### Repositories Compressing and Filtering Tool Output

Several repositories and frameworks optimize context windows for AI coding agents by filtering, sandboxing, or compressing tool outputs:

1. **`context-mode` (`mksglu/context-mode`)**: An MCP server and multi-platform plugin system that sandboxes tool output before it enters the context window [1, 2]. It runs code in isolated subprocesses (supporting 12 languages), captures `stdout`, and indexes heavy outputs into SQLite FTS5, preventing raw log files, API responses, and browser snapshots from clogging the LLM context [2-5].
2. **`RTK` (`@terrain-ai/rtk`)**: Integrated into the **Terrain** engineering environment (`sopaco/terrain`) as part of its agent navigation layer [6, 7]. RTK acts as a dedicated CLI tool that compresses shell command output to save tokens during agent execution [7, 8].
3. **`billion-context` (`ranxianglei/billion-context`)**: An incremental, hierarchical context-compression proxy (`acp-kernel`) that sits between AI coding agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor) and model APIs [9, 10]. It introduces model-driven context management tools (`compress`, `decompress`, `search_context`, `acp_status`) so the model itself folds older context into high-fidelity summaries [10, 11].
4. **`LeanCTX` (`yvgude/lean-ctx`)**: A local "Context Gateway" for AI systems that provides 16 structured file read modes (such as `map`, `signatures`, and `density:0.4`) and filters shell output using 85+ command output patterns (for `git`, `npm`, `cargo`, `docker`, `kubectl`, etc.) [12, 13].
5. **`XERJ` (`xerj-org/xerj`)**: An auto-indexing code and data search engine that uses tree-sitter AST parsing and trigram search to deliver targeted code passages rather than dumping whole files or large `grep` outputs into the prompt [14-16].
6. **`Trail-Code` (`trailhq/Trail-Code`)**: Formerly known as Graft, it uses a tree-sitter code map and session learnings to give agents immediate access to relevant functions and call dependencies, eliminating repetitive grepping and file discovery [17-19].

---

### Integration Mechanics with Claude Code: `PreToolUse` vs `PostToolUse`

Tools like `context-mode` integrate with Claude Code and other coding agent platforms (such as Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and Kiro) by leveraging lifecycle hooks [20-22].

#### 1. `PreToolUse` (Command Rewrite & Pre-Execution Routing)
* **Execution Phase**: Fires **before** a tool call runs [21, 22].
* **Functionality**:
  * **Command Blocking & Redirection**: Intercepts high-volume or "high-flood" commands (e.g., raw `Bash`, `curl`, `Read`, `Grep`, or Playwright snapshots) and blocks or redirects them to sandboxed alternatives (`ctx_execute`, `ctx_batch_execute`) [3, 21, 23, 24].
  * **Input Rewriting (`updatedInput`)**: On platforms that support payload modification (such as Claude Code and Kimi Code), `PreToolUse` can rewrite tool arguments on the fly before execution [22, 25, 26]. On platforms with narrower hook capabilities (such as Codex CLI), `PreToolUse` supports `deny` (blocking) decisions while waiting for upstream `updatedInput` support [25, 27].
  * **Guidance Re-injection**: Re-injects prompt guidance periodically (e.g., every 10th tool call) reminding the agent to wrap large external payloads in sandboxed tools [23].

#### 2. `PostToolUse` (Output Capture & Event Extraction)
* **Execution Phase**: Fires **after** a tool completes execution [21, 22].
* **Functionality**:
  * **Event Logging & Extraction**: Captures structured metadata from the completed tool call—such as edited file paths, git operations, CLI execution latency, and error states—storing them in a project-level SQLite database without dumping raw output into the active chat transcript [21, 28].
  * **Context-Safe Summarization**: When tool output exceeds a threshold (e.g., 5 KB in `context-mode`), `PostToolUse` triggers intent-driven filtering, indexing the full raw output into a SQLite FTS5 database and returning only a focused matching snippet alongside searchable terms [5].

---

### Quantitative Token Reductions & Measurement Methodologies

| Repository | Measured Reduction | How It Is Measured |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`context-mode`** | **98% overall context reduction** (315 KB raw tool output reduced to 5.4 KB) [2, 3, 29]. | Compares raw input/output bytes against the compact `stdout` or FTS5 snippet returned to the chat context [2, 3, 5]. Reported live via `/context-mode:ctx-stats`, the `context-mode statusline`, or `ctx stats` [20, 30, 31]. |
| **`billion-context`** | **5x fewer tokens**; maintains a **95–97% prefix-cache hit rate** [32, 33]. | Measured via a 4.5-month longitudinal study tracking 174,327 model calls and 18.76 billion tokens [9]. Per-turn cache health is calculated as `[acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%)` and audited via `/__bili/cache-report` [33, 34]. |
| **`XERJ`** | **2.7x–5x fewer tokens** compared to `grep`-driven agents (up to **278x fewer** on individual tasks) [14]. | Benchmarked end-to-end on unmemorized codebase tasks comparing memory-only, `grep`-driven, and XERJ retrieval token counts and costs [14]. |
| **`Trail-Code`** | **42% fewer uncached input tokens**, **46% fewer tool calls**, and **32% lower cost** [18, 35]. | Measured across 162 multi-file task benchmark runs and 50 SWE-bench Verified instances comparing cold agents against map-assisted agents [18, 35, 36]. |
| **`LeanCTX`** | Variable savings across 85+ shell command patterns and 16 read modes [13]. | Utilizes a "Shadow Mode" baseline engine (`lean-ctx shadow` / `lean-ctx savings`) that simulates what uncompressed tool outputs would have cost to calculate token and cost deltas [37-39]. |

#### Specific Output Reduction Benchmarks (`context-mode`):
* **Playwright HTML Snapshot**: 56.2 KB → 299 B (**99% saved**) [29].
* **GitHub Issues (20 items)**: 58.9 KB → 1.1 KB (**98% saved**) [29].
* **Access Log (500 requests)**: 45.1 KB → 155 B (**100% saved**) [29].
* **Analytics CSV (500 rows)**: 85.5 KB → 222 B (**100% saved**) [29].
* **Large JSON API (20,000 records)**: 7.5 MB → 0.9 KB (**99% saved**) [40].

---

### How These Tools Avoid Hiding Failures

Filtering and compressing tool output carries the risk of swallowing critical error details, stack traces, or non-zero exit codes. These repositories implement several mechanisms to ensure failures remain visible to the agent:

1. **Dedicated Error Event Extraction in `PostToolUse`**:
   * In `context-mode`, tool failures, non-zero exit codes, and error traces are explicitly categorized as **High Priority (P2) events** [28].
   * The system detects sequential "Error → Fix" pairs across tool calls, ensuring that error context is indexed into FTS5 for immediate retrieval rather than lost during compaction [28, 41].
2. **Preservation of `stdout`/`stderr` Streams in Code Execution**:
   * Sandboxed execution tools (like `ctx_execute`) execute code in isolated subprocesses and return the script's `stdout` and error output directly to the LLM [4]. The LLM sees full runtime error messages and stack traces whenever a script fails [4].
3. **Intent-Driven Fallback for Large Output**:
   * When output exceeds 5 KB, `context-mode` does not truncate blindly; it indexes the entire output into SQLite FTS5 and extracts matching sections based on intent, returning the relevant snippets along with searchable terms so the agent can query specific error lines if needed [5].
4. **Reversible & Model-Driven Decompression**:
   * In `billion-context`, summaries are written incrementally and can be decompressed on demand using the `decompress` tool if exact original error text is needed [11, 42].
   * In `LeanCTX`, compact views retain source and archive references for expansion via `ctx_expand` or `ctx_retrieve` [13]. Users can also bypass compression for specific commands using `lean-ctx -c --raw "<command>"` when raw unformatted logs are required [43].
5. **Fail-Open Behavior**:
   * If hook scripts fail or encounter version mismatches, tools like `context-mode` fail open rather than blocking tool execution or hiding command results [44]. Boundary violations (e.g., attempted out-of-workspace file reads) return explicit, actionable error messages ("File access blocked") [45].

---

How Context Mode Solves It Context Mode is an MCP server that solves all four sides of this problem: Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction. Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't --continue , previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate. Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 17 supported clients, plus the OpenClaw gateway integration: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator.

references.cited_text: How the Sandbox Works Each ctx_execute call spawns an isolated subprocess with its own process boundary. Scripts can't access each other's memory or state. The subprocess runs your code, captures stdout, and only that stdout enters the conversation context. The raw data — log files, API responses, snapshots — never leaves the sandbox. Twelve language runtimes are available: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Shell, Ruby, Go, Rust, PHP, Perl, R, Elixir, and C#. Bun is auto-detected for 3-5x faster JS/TS execution.

Authenticated CLIs work through credential passthrough — gh , aws , gcloud , kubectl , docker inherit environment variables and config paths without exposing them to the conversation. When output exceeds 5 KB and an intent is provided, Context Mode switches to intent-driven filtering: it indexes the full output into the knowledge base, searches for sections matching your intent, and returns only the relevant matches with a vocabulary of searchable terms for follow-up queries. How the Knowledge Base Works The ctx_index tool chunks markdown content by headings while keeping code blocks intact, then stores them in a SQLite FTS5 (Full-Text Search 5) virtual table. The SQLite backend is selected automatically at runtime: bun:sqlite on Bun, node:sqlite on Node.js >= 22.5, and better-sqlite3 everywhere else. Search uses BM25 ranking — a probabilistic relevance algorithm that scores documents based on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. Porter stemming is applied at index time so "running", "runs", and "ran" match the same stem. Titles and headings are weighted 5x in BM25 scoring for precise navigational queries.

Part 1: The graft map Without a map, your coding agent starts every task blind. It greps a term, opens a file, follows an import, backs out and tries again, rebuilding a picture of a codebase it mapped an hour ago and threw away. That rediscovery burns most of a run's tool calls, tokens and time. People onboard to a codebase once. Agents onboard every single time. The graft map builds that understanding once, and keeps it current: Every file, function and caller. Parsed with tree-sitter into a graph of symbols and who calls what. Deterministic, no model, no network, 23 languages. The right code with every prompt. In Claude Code, hooks add the matching files and functions to each prompt, and show what depends on a file right after your agent edits it (the "blast radius"). Cursor, Codex and other agents get the same map through MCP tools and their instruction files. Always fresh. Every query checks the working tree first (a few tens of milliseconds when nothing moved) and rebuilds only what changed, so answers describe the code as it is right now, uncommitted edits included. Plain files you can read. Linked markdown nodes your agent opens and greps like any other file. No embeddings, no index to keep warm. Usage and cost — measure the result Context controls and evidence come first. Usage estimates and calculated costs help you assess their operational effect; they do not prove answer quality. Shadow Mode — a simulated baseline Shadow Mode estimates what the same work would have cost without LeanCTX, without changing the active workflow. The baseline is simulated from the uncompressed token counts and the same outcome signals, not a second measured run, so its reports estimate cost, tokens and CPAO deltas; they do not measure answer quality.

LeanCTX records local cost and outcome signals without adding those reports to agent context. CPAO (cost per accepted outcome) is one comparison metric; Shadow Mode provides simulated savings estimates. Keep estimates, provider-measured usage and outcome quality separate.

Why Long coding sessions blow up context. Each provider charges per token, and once you pass the context window the session degrades or dies. billion-context compresses consumed conversation into layered summaries so you can run a single session for days — billions of tokens through one context window. Unlike a host's built-in summarizer, compression here is incremental, reversible, and prefix-cache friendly : summaries are written in small ranges, can be decompressed on demand, and the cache prefix stays intact.

The pattern is Tool(what to match) where * means "anything". Commands chained with && , ; , or | are split — each part is checked separately. echo hello && sudo rm -rf /tmp is blocked because the sudo part matches the deny rule. deny always wins over allow . More specific (project-level) rules override global ones. Project-boundary containment ctx_execute_file is confined to the project root. A path that resolves outside the workspace — an absolute path like /home/user/secrets , a ../../ traversal, or a project-local symlink whose target escapes the project — is refused with a File access blocked error. This closes the #852 escape vector where an agent, denied an out-of-project read by the host sandbox, retried through the MCP sandbox (the host's MCP approval prompt cannot inspect the tool's input params, so the escape was invisible to the approver).
